title: The Moving Point of Light
text:
In the mid-1930s, at Columbia University, the young Turkish psychologist Muzafer Sherif used a quirk of human vision. In a completely dark room, a small, fixed point of light seems to drift, because the eye has nothing to anchor it. This is called the autokinetic effect. How far the light appears to move is pure guesswork.

Sherif asked people to estimate, again and again, how many inches the light moved. Alone, each person soon settled on a personal range of answers, and these ranges differed widely from one person to the next. Then he brought people into the dark room in twos and threes and had them call out their estimates in turn.

Over a few sessions, the estimates within each group drew together until the group shared a common range, its own norm for a movement that did not actually exist. Different groups settled on different norms. Most striking of all, when people who had formed a norm in a group were later tested alone, they kept using the group's figure rather than returning to their original answers.

Sherif concluded that when reality is unclear, people build shared frames of reference together, and those frames then live on inside each member.
lesson: Where facts are fuzzy, a team quietly invents its own standards. Check which of your group's habits rest on evidence and which only rest on having been repeated together.
source: Sherif, M. (1935). A study of some social factors in perception. Archives of Psychology.
